subsystems.name: Cell source and expansion
subsystems.role: provides patient-matched cells to build the organ.

subsystems.name: Bioink and extracellular matrix
subsystems.role: carries cells and forms the temporary scaffolding.

subsystems.name: Bioprinting system
subsystems.role: deposits bioinks precisely, layer by layer.

subsystems.name: Vascular network
subsystems.role: supplies every cell with oxygen and nutrients, without which thick tissue dies.

subsystems.name: Maturation bioreactor
subsystems.role: conditions the printed construct to become functional tissue.

subsystems.name: Quality control and surgical interface
subsystems.role: verifies the organ is safe and connects it to the patient.

buildSteps.title: Harvest patient cells
buildSteps.detail: A small skin or blood sample is taken; cells are reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells so they match the patient and avoid rejection.

buildSteps.title: Expand and differentiate
buildSteps.detail: The stem cells are grown in large numbers and steered with chemical signals into the organ's specialised cells — for example heart muscle, liver or kidney cells.

buildSteps.title: Map the organ
buildSteps.detail: Medical scans are converted into a digital 3D model that includes the organ's shape and its branching blood vessels.

buildSteps.title: Formulate bioinks
buildSteps.detail: Cells are mixed into a hydrogel that keeps them alive and printable; separate sacrificial inks are prepared to create the vessel channels.

buildSteps.title: Print the organ
buildSteps.detail: The bioprinter lays down thousands of thin layers, switching between cell-laden inks and sacrificial support, following the digital model.

buildSteps.title: Create the vasculature
buildSteps.detail: The sacrificial ink is dissolved away, leaving hollow channels; endothelial cells are then flowed in to line them and form blood-vessel walls.

buildSteps.title: Mature in a bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: The organ is perfused with oxygen and nutrients for days or weeks, with mechanical cues that help the cells organise into working tissue.

buildSteps.title: Test and implant
buildSteps.detail: The organ is checked for sterility and function, then surgically connected to the patient's blood supply and, for some organs, to ducts or other outlets.

prerequisites.why: iPSC technology exists, but growing enough cells for a whole organ is not yet routine.
no engineered tissue more than a few millimetres thick survives without a built-in blood supply.
current printers cannot yet place capillaries at the density of real organs quickly enough.
hydrogels can hold cells but often lack the strength and signals of natural tissue.
perfusion systems exist for small tissues but scaling to a whole heart or kidney is unresolved.

pathway.milestone: bioprinted tissues and organoids used for drug testing and disease modelling; simple flat or tubular structures are in early clinical study
pathway.unlocks: better drugs and fewer animal tests.

pathway.milestone: bioprinted patches and small organ units that can survive when implanted
pathway.unlocks: repair of damaged organs rather than full replacement.

pathway.milestone: whole simple organs or scaled-up solid organs with integrated vasculature proven in large animals
pathway.unlocks: first human trials for selected organs.

pathway.milestone: on-demand manufacturing of patient-specific solid organs in automated facilities
pathway.unlocks: an end to organ waiting lists and lifelong immunosuppression for many patients.
